content: Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (EIB) is a condition that occurs after intense physical activity, leading to symptoms such as coughing, shortness of breath, wheezing, and chest tightness. This condition can negatively impact physical performance and may discourage individuals from engaging in physical activity. The management of EIB typically involves preventive measures, including pharmacological treatments and other strategies. Commonly recommended medications include single-use, pre-exercise beta-agonists and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents. Bronchodilators are frequently used to prevent airway narrowing after exercise. However, anti-inflammatory drugs like nedocromil sodium have also been employed for this purpose. The aim of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of a single dose of nedocromil sodium in preventing EIB. To gather relevant data, researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Airways Group Specialised Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and other sources such as review articles, textbooks, and reference lists. They also contacted the drug manufacturer and primary authors for additional information. The search was last updated in August 2008. The review included randomized controlled trials that compared a single dose of nedocromil sodium with a placebo in individuals aged six years or older who had EIB. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the trials and extracted data. Study authors were contacted to confirm the data. No new studies were identified in the updated search conducted in August 2008. The analysis included data from 20 randomized controlled trials involving 280 participants. The results demonstrated that inhaling 4 mg of nedocromil sodium 15 to 60 minutes before exercise significantly reduced the severity and duration of EIB in both adults and children compared to placebo. Specifically, the maximum percentage fall in forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) was significantly improved with nedocromil sodium, with a weighted mean difference (WMD) of 15.5% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 13.2% to 18.1%). Similarly, the maximum percentage fall in peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) showed a WMD of 15.0% (95% CI: 8.3% to 21.6%). Nedocromil sodium also significantly reduced the time required for lung function to return to normal after exercise. While recovery took more than 30 minutes with placebo, it was reduced to less than 10 minutes with nedocromil sodium. The drug was particularly effective in individuals with more severe EIB, defined as a greater than 30% reduction in lung function from baseline after exercise. Importantly, no significant adverse effects were reported with the short-term use of nedocromil sodium. In conclusion, the use of nedocromil sodium before exercise effectively reduces the severity and duration of EIB. This benefit is especially pronounced in individuals with severe EIB.
